title: Greet by name
instructorPromptText: Write a program that asks the user for their name, then prints a friendly greeting like 'Hello, Alice!'.

specGateDimensions.description: What exact text surrounds the name in the output — is it 'Hello, <name>!' with a comma and exclamation, or some other phrasing?
specGateDimensions.rationale: The prompt says 'like Hello, Alice!' which is illustrative, not prescriptive. Forcing the student to commit to the exact string they will produce makes Phase 4 diffing possible.

specGateDimensions.description: What text does the program display when asking for the name (e.g. 'What is your name? ')?
specGateDimensions.rationale: Students often leave input() empty and then can't tell if the program is hung. Committing to a prompt string is a small but real interface decision.

specGateDimensions.description: If the user just presses Enter or types spaces, does the program greet them anyway ('Hello, !') or is the program allowed to assume the user types a real name?
specGateDimensions.rationale: At unit_1 the student has no if/else, so 'assume the user types a real name' is an acceptable commitment — but naming that assumption explicitly is the pedagogical point.

expectedDivergences.pattern: Spec commits to the format 'Hello, <name>!' but code prints 'Hello <name>' (missing comma or exclamation) because the student eyeballed the example
Student concatenates with + but forgets to include the space/comma, producing 'Hello,Alice!' or 'HelloAlice!'
Plan describes string concatenation with +; code uses an f-string instead — coherent stylistic choice within unit_1 tooling
Student stores the name but prints a literal variable name or the raw input prompt return value without using it
